answers.who: Abaddon, the angel of the bottomless pit and 'destroyer' named in Revelation 9:11, later counted among the orders of devils.
Joachim of Fiore (c. 1135–1202), Calabrian abbot whose apocalyptic prophecies of a coming age of the Spirit were widely cited.
Battle Abbey, Sussex, built on the site of the Battle of Hastings (1066).
Abdalonymus, poor gardener of royal descent whom Alexander the Great made king of Sidon, as told by Quintus Curtius.
Abdera, Greek city on the coast of Thrace, home of Democritus; its people were proverbial for stupidity.
The Abderites, citizens of Abdera in Thrace, who in the pseudo-Hippocratic letters sent for Hippocrates to cure Democritus of supposed madness.
Abderus, favourite of Hercules in Greek myth, killed by the man-eating mares of Diomedes; Abdera was said to be named after him.
Abel, son of Adam, murdered by his brother Cain (Genesis 4); also named in the title of Ambrose's treatise De Cain et Abel.
Abigail, wife of the churlish Nabal, who placated David and later married him (1 Samuel 25).

answers.who: Abraham, the Hebrew patriarch, husband of Sarah; 'Abraham men' (second passage) were vagrant beggars who feigned madness.
Abraham ibn Ezra (c. 1089–c. 1164), Spanish Jewish biblical commentator, astrologer and scholar.
Abraham Ortelius (1527–1598), Antwerp cartographer, compiler of the atlas Theatrum Orbis Terrarum.

answers.who: Absalom, son of King David, who rebelled against his father and was killed; David mourned him (2 Samuel 13–18).
Apsyrtus, brother of Medea in Greek myth, whom she killed and dismembered to delay their father Aeetes' pursuit of the Argonauts.
Alfonso Tostado (c. 1400–1455), 'Abulensis', bishop of Ávila, Spanish theologian and voluminous biblical commentator.
Abydos, ancient Greek city on the Asian shore of the Hellespont (Dardanelles).
The Abyssinians, people of the Christian empire of Ethiopia, whose ruler Europeans identified with Prester John.

Acarnania, region of western Greece on the Ionian Sea, bordering the Ambracian Gulf.

answers.who: Acco, proverbial foolish old woman of Greek tradition who went mad on seeing her aged face in a mirror; used as a bogey.
Acestes, Trojan-descended king in Sicily in Virgil's Aeneid, whose arrow caught fire in flight during the funeral games (Book 5).

answers.who: Achaea, region of the northern Peloponnese, Greece; also the Roman name for the province covering southern Greece.
Achaica, Book 7 of Pausanias' Description of Greece, covering Achaea.
Achan, Israelite who stole a Babylonian garment and gold from Jericho, bringing disaster on Israel, and was stoned (Joshua 7).
Achan, Israelite stoned for stealing devoted spoil at Jericho (Joshua 7); used figuratively for church robbers.
Aachen (Aix-la-Chapelle), city in western Germany, Charlemagne's residence and burial place.
Achelous, Greek river god who wrestled Hercules for Deianira and lost a horn.
Achilles, greatest Greek hero of the Trojan War in Homer's Iliad; his spear both wounded and healed Telephus.
Achilles, Greek hero of the Iliad, whose glory Alexander the Great sought to emulate.
Ahithophel, David's counsellor who joined Absalom's revolt and hanged himself when his advice was rejected (2 Samuel 15–17).

Gedik Ahmed Pasha (d. 1482), Ottoman grand vizier and general, executed by Sultan Bayezid II.
Acre (Akko), port in present-day northern Israel, besieged and taken by the Third Crusade (1189–1191).
